prompt:
Let $\mathbb Z$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$f(2a)+2f(b)=f\big(f(a+b)\big).$$
answer: $f(x)=0$ for all $x$, and $f(x)=2x+c$ for any integer constant $c$.

prompt:
Let $u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{2019}$ be real numbers satisfying
$$u_1+u_2+\dots+u_{2019}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad u_1^2+u_2^2+\dots+u_{2019}^2=1.$$
Let $a=\min(u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{2019})$ and $b=\max(u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{2019})$. Prove that
$$ab\le-\frac1{2019}.$$
answer: Proof: split the indices into positive ($p$ of them) and nonpositive ($n$ of them) terms; $\sum_P u_i^2\le b\sum_P u_i=b\sum_N|u_i|\le -nab$ and $\sum_N u_i^2\le -pab$, so $1\le-2019ab$.

solutions.title: Bound the squares of each sign separately
solutions.body:
**$a<0<b$.** The squares sum to $1$, so not all $u_i$ are $0$; the sum is $0$, so the nonzero ones cannot all have the same sign. Hence $a<0<b$.

Let $P=\{i:u_i>0\}$ and $N=\{i:u_i\le0\}$, with $p=|P|$, $n=|N|$, so $p+n=2019$. The condition $\sum u_i=0$ says
$$\sum_{i\in P}u_i=\sum_{i\in N}|u_i|.\tag{1}$$

For $i\in P$ we have $0<u_i\le b$, so $u_i^2\le b\,u_i$. For $i\in N$ we have $0\le|u_i|\le|a|$, so $u_i^2\le|a|\,|u_i|$. Using (1),
$$\sum_{i\in P}u_i^2\le b\sum_{i\in P}u_i=b\sum_{i\in N}|u_i|\le b\cdot n|a|=-nab,$$
$$\sum_{i\in N}u_i^2\le|a|\sum_{i\in N}|u_i|=|a|\sum_{i\in P}u_i\le|a|\cdot pb=-pab.$$
Adding the two estimates,
$$1=\sum_{i=1}^{2019}u_i^2\le-(p+n)ab=-2019ab,$$
which is $ab\le-\frac1{2019}$. ∎

solutions.title: Write each $u_i$ as a mix of $a$ and $b$
solutions.body:
As before $a<0<b$. Each $u_i$ lies in $[a,b]$, so $u_i=x_ia+y_ib$ with $x_i,y_i\ge0$, $x_i+y_i=1$. Put $X=\sum x_i$, $Y=\sum y_i$. Then
$$X+Y=2019,\qquad 0=\sum u_i=aX+bY\ \Rightarrow\ |a|X=bY,$$
so $X=\dfrac{2019\,b}{|a|+b}$ and $Y=\dfrac{2019\,|a|}{|a|+b}$.

Since $0\le x_i,y_i\le1$ and $ab<0$,
$$u_i^2=x_i^2a^2+2x_iy_iab+y_i^2b^2\le x_ia^2+y_ib^2.$$
Summing,
$$1\le Xa^2+Yb^2=\frac{2019\,(b\,a^2+|a|\,b^2)}{|a|+b}=\frac{2019\,|a|b\,(|a|+b)}{|a|+b}=-2019ab.$$
∎

prompt:
Let $n\ge3$ be a positive integer and let $(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n)$ be a strictly increasing sequence of $n$ positive real numbers with sum equal to $2$. Let $X$ be a subset of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ such that the value of
$$\Big|1-\sum_{i\in X}a_i\Big|$$
is minimised. Prove that there exists a strictly increasing sequence of $n$ positive real numbers $(b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n)$ with sum equal to $2$ such that
$$\sum_{i\in X}b_i=1.$$
answer: Proof: WLOG $\sum_X a_i<1$ and put $\Delta=\sum_{X^c}a_i-\sum_X a_i>0$. Minimality forces $a_{j+1}-a_j\ge\Delta$ whenever $j\in X$, $j+1\notin X$ (and $a_1\ge\Delta$ if $X=\{k,\dots,n\}$); then move $\Delta/2$ from $a_{j+1}$ to $a_j$ (or from $a_1$ to $a_n$), with a tiny extra shift $\varepsilon$ in the equality case.

solutions.title: Perturb two neighbouring terms
solutions.body:
Write $X^c$ for the complement of $X$ and
$$\Delta=\sum_{i\in X^c}a_i-\sum_{i\in X}a_i .$$
Since $\sum_X a_i+\sum_{X^c}a_i=2$, we have $1-\sum_X a_i=\Delta/2$, so $X$ minimises $|\Delta|$ among all index sets, and $|1-\sum_X a_i|=|1-\sum_{X^c}a_i|$. Hence we may swap $X$ and $X^c$. If $\Delta=0$ take $b_i=a_i$. Otherwise, swapping if necessary, assume $\Delta>0$, i.e. $\sum_X a_i=1-\frac\Delta2<1$. We want strictly increasing positive $b_i$ with the same total $2$ and $\sum_X b_i=\sum_X a_i+\frac\Delta2$.

Note that $X\ne\varnothing$: for $X=\varnothing$ the value is $1$, while $X=\{n\}$ gives $|1-a_n|<1$ because $0<a_n<2$. Also $X\neq\{1,\dots,n\}$ because $\sum_X a_i<1$.

**Case 1: some $j\le n-1$ has $j\in X$, $j+1\notin X$.** Replacing $X$ by $X'=X\cup\{j+1\}\setminus\{j\}$ changes $\Delta$ to $\Delta'=\Delta-2\delta$, where $\delta=a_{j+1}-a_j>0$. If $\delta<\Delta$ then $|\Delta'|<\Delta$, contradicting minimality. So $\delta\ge\Delta$.

* If $\delta>\Delta$: put $b_j=a_j+\frac\Delta2$, $b_{j+1}=a_{j+1}-\frac\Delta2$, and $b_i=a_i$ otherwise. Then $b_{j+1}-b_j=\delta-\Delta>0$, $b_j>a_j>a_{j-1}$ and $b_{j+1}<a_{j+1}<a_{j+2}$, so the sequence is still strictly increasing and positive. The total is unchanged and $\sum_X b_i$ went up by $\frac\Delta2$.
* If $\delta=\Delta$: the previous choice would give $b_j=b_{j+1}$, so we shift a little extra. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than $\frac\Delta2$, than $a_1$, and than every difference $a_{i+1}-a_i$. Since $n\ge3$, $|X|\ge2$ or $|X^c|\ge2$.
  * If $|X|\ge2$, pick $k\in X$, $k\ne j$, and put $b_j=a_j+\frac\Delta2-\varepsilon$, $b_{j+1}=a_{j+1}-\frac\Delta2$, $b_k=a_k+\varepsilon$, and $b_i=a_i$ otherwise. Then $\sum_X b_i$ rises by $\frac\Delta2$ and the total is unchanged. For monotonicity: $b_{j+1}-b_j=\varepsilon>0$; $b_j>a_j$ because $\varepsilon<\frac\Delta2$; and $a_k<b_k<a_{k+1}$ because $\varepsilon<a_{k+1}-a_k$. (If $k+1=j$ then $b_k<a_j<b_j$.) Positivity is clear.
  * If $|X^c|\ge2$, pick $k\in X^c$, $k\ne j+1$, and put $b_j=a_j+\frac\Delta2$, $b_{j+1}=a_{j+1}-\frac\Delta2+\varepsilon$, $b_k=a_k-\varepsilon$, and $b_i=a_i$ otherwise. Again $\sum_X b_i$ rises by $\frac\Delta2$ and the total is unchanged. We have $b_{j+1}-b_j=\varepsilon>0$ and $a_{k-1}<b_k<a_k$, and $b_k>0$ since $\varepsilon<a_1$. If $k-1=j+1$, then $b_k-b_{j+1}=(a_k-a_{j+1})-2\varepsilon+\frac\Delta2>(a_k-a_{j+1})-\varepsilon>0$.

**Case 2: no such $j$.** Then $X$ is "closed upwards": $X=\{k,k+1,\dots,n\}$ for some $k\ge2$. Adding the index $1$ to $X$ changes $\Delta$ to $\Delta-2a_1$. If $a_1<\Delta$, this has absolute value less than $\Delta$, which is impossible. So $a_1\ge\Delta$. Put $b_1=a_1-\frac\Delta2>0$, $b_n=a_n+\frac\Delta2$, and $b_i=a_i$ otherwise. Since $n\ge3$, $b_1<a_1<a_2$ and $b_n>a_n>a_{n-1}$, so the sequence is strictly increasing. The total is unchanged and $\sum_X b_i$ rises by $\frac\Delta2$ (as $n\in X$, $1\notin X$).

In every case $\sum_X b_i=1-\frac\Delta2+\frac\Delta2=1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n\ge2$ be a positive integer and $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ be real numbers such that
$$a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n=0.$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$A=\big\{(i,j)\ \big|\ 1\le i<j\le n,\ |a_i-a_j|\ge1\big\}.$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$\sum_{(i,j)\in A}a_ia_j<0.$$
answer: Proof: over ordered pairs, $\sum_A a_ia_j=-\frac12\sum_{|a_i-a_j|<1}a_ia_j$. The sum over close pairs is at least $\sum_{|a_i|\ge1}a_i^2+\big(\sum_{|a_i|<1}a_i\big)^2\ge0$, and the inequality is strict when $A\neq\varnothing$.

solutions.title: Pass to the complementary set of close pairs
solutions.body:
Use ordered pairs. Let
$$B=\{(i,j):1\le i,j\le n,\ |a_i-a_j|\ge1\},\qquad C=\{(i,j):1\le i,j\le n,\ |a_i-a_j|<1\}.$$
Pairs $(i,i)$ lie in $C$, and $B$ consists of the pairs of $A$ in both orders, so $\sum_A a_ia_j=\frac12\sum_B a_ia_j$. Also
$$\sum_B a_ia_j=\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j-\sum_C a_ia_j=\Big(\sum_i a_i\Big)^2-\sum_C a_ia_j=-\sum_C a_ia_j.$$
So it suffices to show that $\sum_C a_ia_j>0$ when $A\ne\varnothing$.

Split the indices into
$$P=\{i:a_i\le-1\},\quad Q=\{i:-1<a_i\le0\},\quad R=\{i:0<a_i<1\},\quad S=\{i:a_i\ge1\}.$$

**Claim.**
$$\sum_{(i,j)\in C}a_ia_j\ \ge\ \sum_{i\in P\cup S}a_i^2+\sum_{i,j\in Q\cup R}a_ia_j\ =\ \sum_{i\in P\cup S}a_i^2+\Big(\sum_{i\in Q\cup R}a_i\Big)^2\ \ge0 .$$

Call the right-hand side before the equals sign $\Sigma_{\text{RHS}}$. Compare positive and negative terms.

* Every positive term of $\Sigma_{\text{RHS}}$ also occurs in $\sum_C$. The terms $a_i^2$ with $i\in P\cup S$ come from the pairs $(i,i)\in C$. A positive product $a_ia_j$ with $i,j\in Q\cup R$ has $i,j$ both in $Q$ or both in $R$. Each of those intervals has length at most $1$ and is half-open, so $|a_i-a_j|<1$ and $(i,j)\in C$.
* Every negative term of $\sum_C$ also occurs in $\Sigma_{\text{RHS}}$. If $a_ia_j<0$ and $|a_i-a_j|<1$, the two numbers have opposite signs and differ by less than $1$, so both lie in $(-1,1)$, i.e. $i,j\in Q\cup R$.

All other terms of $\sum_C$ are $\ge0$ and all other terms of $\Sigma_{\text{RHS}}$ are $\le0$. So $\sum_C\ge(\text{positive part of }\Sigma_{\text{RHS}})+(\text{negative part of }\textstyle\sum_C)\ge\Sigma_{\text{RHS}}$, which proves the claim.

**Strictness.** Suppose $A\ne\varnothing$. If $P\cup S\neq\varnothing$, the last inequality is strict because $\sum_{P\cup S}a_i^2>0$. If $P=S=\varnothing$, all $a_i\in(-1,1)$. Take $(i,j)\in A$, so $|a_i-a_j|\ge1$. As shown above, this pair cannot lie in the same one of $Q$ and $R$, so one is in $Q$ and one in $R$. Moreover, the one in $Q$ is not $0$, since otherwise the difference would be less than $1$. So $a_ia_j<0$ is a negative term of $\Sigma_{\text{RHS}}$ that is missing from $\sum_C$, and the first inequality is strict.

Hence $\sum_C a_ia_j>0$, and $\sum_A a_ia_j=-\frac12\sum_C a_ia_j<0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$ be different real numbers. Prove that
$$\sum_{1\le i\le n}\ \prod_{j\ne i}\frac{1-x_ix_j}{x_i-x_j}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $n$ is even;}\\[2pt]1,&\text{if $n$ is odd.}\end{cases}$$
answer: Proof: interpolate $f(t)=\prod_i(1-x_it)$ (degree $n$) at the $n+2$ nodes $x_1,\dots,x_n,1,-1$; the coefficient of $t^{n+1}$ in the Lagrange formula is $0=-G+\frac12+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}2$, where $G$ is the given sum.

solutions.title: Lagrange interpolation with two extra nodes
solutions.body:
Let $G(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ be the left-hand side. It is a continuous function on the set of $n$-tuples of distinct reals, and the tuples with no $x_i=\pm1$ are dense in that set. So it suffices to prove the identity when all $x_i\notin\{1,-1\}$.

Let
$$f(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n(1-x_it),$$
a polynomial of degree at most $n$. Note that $f(x_i)=(1-x_i^2)\prod_{j\ne i}(1-x_ix_j)$, $f(1)=\prod_j(1-x_j)$ and $f(-1)=\prod_j(1+x_j)$.

The $n+2$ numbers $x_1,\dots,x_n,1,-1$ are distinct. By Lagrange interpolation, $f$ equals the unique polynomial of degree $\le n+1$ through these nodes. Its coefficient of $t^{n+1}$ is
$$\sum_{\text{nodes }u}\frac{f(u)}{\prod_{v\ne u}(u-v)} .$$
This coefficient is $0$ because $\deg f\le n$. Compute the three kinds of terms:

* node $x_i$: $\displaystyle\frac{(1-x_i^2)\prod_{j\ne i}(1-x_ix_j)}{\prod_{j\ne i}(x_i-x_j)\,(x_i-1)(x_i+1)}=-\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{1-x_ix_j}{x_i-x_j}$;
* node $1$: $\displaystyle\frac{\prod_j(1-x_j)}{\prod_j(1-x_j)\cdot(1+1)}=\frac12$;
* node $-1$: $\displaystyle\frac{\prod_j(1+x_j)}{\prod_j(-1-x_j)\cdot(-1-1)}=\frac{1}{(-1)^n\cdot(-2)}=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}2$.

Hence
$$0=-G+\frac12+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad G=\frac{1+(-1)^{n+1}}2,$$
which is $0$ for even $n$ and $1$ for odd $n$. ∎

prompt:
A polynomial $P(x,y,z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$P(x,y,z)=P(x,y,xy-z)=P(x,zx-y,z)=P(yz-x,y,z).$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$P(x,y,z)=F(x^2+y^2+z^2-xyz).$$
answer: Proof: $P(x,y,z)=P(x,y,xy-z)$ forces $P$ to be a polynomial in $x,y,z(xy-z)$, so every top-degree monomial $x^ay^bz^c$ has $a,b\ge c$; by symmetry $a=b=c$, so the top part is $\mu(xyz)^c$. Subtract $\mu(xyz-x^2-y^2-z^2)^c$ and induct on the degree.

solutions.title: Leading monomials and induction on the degree
solutions.body:
Call $P$ *weakly symmetric* if $P(x,y,z)=P(x,y,xy-z)$. The polynomial $Q=x^2+y^2+z^2-xyz$ satisfies all three identities, and so does every polynomial in $Q$.

**Step 1. A weakly symmetric $P$ is a polynomial in $x$, $y$ and $z(xy-z)$.** Put $P_1(x,y,z)=P\big(x,y,z+\tfrac12xy\big)$. Then
$$P_1(x,y,-z)=P\big(x,y,\tfrac12xy-z\big)=P\big(x,y,xy-(\tfrac12xy-z)\big)=P_1(x,y,z),$$
so $P_1$ is even in $z$. Grouping by powers of $z$, the odd powers must have zero coefficients, so $P_1$ is a polynomial in $x,y,z^2$. Hence $P(x,y,z)=P_1(x,y,z-\frac12xy)$ is a polynomial in $x,y$ and
$$\big(z-\tfrac12xy\big)^2=-z(xy-z)+\tfrac14x^2y^2,$$
hence a polynomial in $x,y,z(xy-z)$.

**Step 2. In a weakly symmetric $P$, every monomial $\mu x^ay^bz^c$ of highest total degree has $a\ge c$ and $b\ge c$.** Write
$$P=\sum_{i,j,k}\mu_{ijk}\,x^iy^j\big(z(xy-z)\big)^k$$
and let $m=\max\{i+j+3k:\mu_{ijk}\ne0\}$. The summand $x^iy^j(z(xy-z))^k$ has degree $i+j+3k$, and its top-degree part is the single monomial $x^{i+k}y^{j+k}z^k$, coming from $(xyz)^k$. Different triples $(i,j,k)$ give different monomials, since $k$ is read off from the exponent of $z$. So the degree-$m$ part of $P$ is $\sum_{i+j+3k=m}\mu_{ijk}x^{i+k}y^{j+k}z^k\ne0$, and each of its monomials has $a=i+k\ge c=k$ and $b=j+k\ge c$.

**Step 3. Induction on $\deg P$.** If $\deg P=0$, $P$ is constant. Otherwise, $P$ is weakly symmetric in each of the three variables: the other two identities say the same thing with the roles of the variables permuted. By Step 2 applied three times, every top-degree monomial $x^ay^bz^c$ satisfies $a,b\ge c$, $a,c\ge b$ and $b,c\ge a$, so $a=b=c$. Thus the top-degree part of $P$ is a single term $\mu(xyz)^c$.

The polynomial $\big(xyz-x^2-y^2-z^2\big)^c=(-Q)^c$ has top-degree part $(xyz)^c$. So
$$P_0=P-\mu(-Q)^c$$
satisfies the three identities and has smaller degree. By induction $P_0=F_0(Q)$ for some polynomial $F_0$, and then $P=F(Q)$ with $F(t)=F_0(t)+\mu(-t)^c$. ∎

prompt:
Let $\mathbb Z$ be the set of integers. We consider functions $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ satisfying
$$f\big(f(x+y)+y\big)=f\big(f(x)+y\big)$$
for all integers $x$ and $y$. For such a function, we say that an integer $v$ is *$f$-rare* if the set
$$X_v=\{x\in\mathbb Z:\ f(x)=v\}$$
is finite and nonempty.

(a) Prove that there exists such a function $f$ for which there is an $f$-rare integer.

(b) Prove that no such function $f$ can have more than one $f$-rare integer.
answer: (a) $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=$ the largest power of $2$ dividing $2x$ for $x\ne0$ works, with $0$ rare. (b) A rare $v$ is a fixed point (use $x=v$, $y=a-v$ and $y=b-v$ with $a,b$ the least/greatest elements of $X_v$); after translating so $v=0$, a second rare $v'$ would satisfy $f(kv')=v'$ for all $k\ge1$.

solutions.title: An explicit example; rare values are fixed points
solutions.body:
**(a)** Define $f(0)=0$, and for $x\ne0$ let $f(x)$ be the largest power of $2$ dividing $2x$. So $f(x)=2$ for odd $x$, every value of $f$ is even, and $f(2x)=2f(x)$ for all $x$. Here $X_0=\{0\}$, so $0$ is $f$-rare.

Check the equation. If $x$ and $y$ are both even, write $x=2x'$, $y=2y'$. Then both sides are twice the corresponding sides for $(x',y')$, since $f(2u)=2f(u)$ and $f(x+y)+y=2(f(x'+y')+y')$. So we may divide by $2$ repeatedly until one of $x,y$ is odd, or $x=y=0$, where the equation is trivial.

* If $y$ is odd: $f(x+y)+y$ and $f(x)+y$ are even plus odd, hence odd, so both sides equal $2$.
* If $x$ is odd and $y$ even: $x+y$ is odd, so $f(x+y)=2=f(x)$ and the two sides are literally equal.

**(b)** *Translation.* If $f$ satisfies the equation, so does $g(x)=f(x+n)-n$ for any integer $n$: indeed $g(g(x+y)+y)=f(f(x+n+y)+y)-n$ and $g(g(x)+y)=f(f(x+n)+y)-n$, which agree by the equation for $f$ at $(x+n,y)$. The rare integers of $g$ are those of $f$ shifted by $-n$.

*A rare integer is a fixed point.* Let $v$ be $f$-rare, and let $a,b$ be the least and greatest elements of $X_v$. Put $x=v$, $y=a-v$: the left side is $f(f(a)+a-v)=f(a)=v$, so $f\big(f(v)+a-v\big)=v$, i.e. $f(v)-v+a\in X_v$. Hence $f(v)-v+a\ge a$, i.e. $f(v)\ge v$. With $y=b-v$ we get likewise $f(v)-v+b\le b$, i.e. $f(v)\le v$. So $f(v)=v$.

*Uniqueness.* Suppose $v\ne v'$ are both rare. Translating, we may assume $v=0$, so $f(0)=0$, and also $f(v')=v'$. We claim $f(kv')=v'$ for all $k\ge1$. This holds for $k=1$. If it holds for $k$, put $x=0$, $y=kv'$:
$$f\big(f(kv')+kv'\big)=f\big(f(0)+kv'\big)\ \Longrightarrow\ f\big((k+1)v'\big)=f(kv')=v'.$$
So $X_{v'}\supseteq\{v',2v',3v',\dots\}$ is infinite (as $v'\ne0$), contradicting rarity. ∎

prompt:
The infinite sequence $a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots$ of (not necessarily different) integers has the following properties: $0\le a_i\le i$ for all integers $i\ge0$, and
$$\binom{k}{a_0}+\binom{k}{a_1}+\dots+\binom{k}{a_k}=2^k$$
for all integers $k\ge0$.

Prove that all integers $N\ge0$ occur in the sequence (that is, for all $N\ge0$, there exists $i\ge0$ with $a_i=N$).
answer: Proof: by induction, for every $k$ the multiset $\{a_0,\dots,a_k\}$ equals $\{0,1,\dots,\ell-1\}\cup\{0,1,\dots,k-\ell\}$ for some $\ell$ with $2\ell\le k+1$ (comparing with $\sum_i\binom{k+1}{i}=2^{k+1}$ forces $\binom{k+1}{a_{k+1}}=\binom{k+1}{\ell}$). Taking $k=2N$ shows $N$ appears among $a_0,\dots,a_{2N}$.

solutions.title: Describe every initial segment
solutions.body:
**Claim.** For every $k\ge0$ there is an $\ell\ge0$ with $2\ell\le k+1$ such that, as multisets,
$$\{a_0,a_1,\dots,a_k\}=\{0,1,\dots,\ell-1\}\cup\{0,1,\dots,k-\ell\}.$$

For $k=0$: $0\le a_0\le0$ gives $a_0=0$, which is the case $\ell=0$.

Suppose the claim holds for $k=m$ with some $\ell$. The condition for $k=m+1$ reads
$$\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}\binom{m+1}{i}+\sum_{i=0}^{m-\ell}\binom{m+1}{i}+\binom{m+1}{a_{m+1}}=2^{m+1}.$$
By symmetry, $\binom{m+1}{i}=\binom{m+1}{m+1-i}$, so the second sum is $\sum_{j=\ell+1}^{m+1}\binom{m+1}{j}$. Together with the first sum, this covers every $j\in\{0,\dots,m+1\}$ except $j=\ell$. Since $\sum_{j=0}^{m+1}\binom{m+1}{j}=2^{m+1}$, we get
$$\binom{m+1}{a_{m+1}}=\binom{m+1}{\ell}.$$
For $0\le i\le m+1$ the binomial coefficients $\binom{m+1}{i}$ strictly increase up to the middle and strictly decrease after it. Since also $0\le a_{m+1}\le m+1$, it follows that $a_{m+1}=\ell$ or $a_{m+1}=m+1-\ell$.

* If $a_{m+1}=m+1-\ell$, the multiset becomes $\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}\cup\{0,\dots,(m+1)-\ell\}$: the claim for $k=m+1$ with the same $\ell$, and $2\ell\le m+1\le m+2$.
* If $a_{m+1}=\ell$ and $2\ell\le m$, the multiset becomes $\{0,\dots,\ell\}\cup\{0,\dots,m-\ell\}$: the claim with $\ell'=\ell+1$, since $(m+1)-\ell'=m-\ell$ and $2\ell'\le m+2$.
* If $a_{m+1}=\ell$ and $2\ell=m+1$, then $\ell=m+1-\ell$, so we are in the first case.

This completes the induction.

**Conclusion.** Given $N\ge0$, apply the claim with $k=2N$. Then $2\ell\le2N+1$ gives $\ell\le N$, so $k-\ell=2N-\ell\ge N$. Hence $N$ belongs to $\{0,1,\dots,k-\ell\}$, i.e. $N=a_i$ for some $i\le2N$. ∎

prompt: You are given a set of $n$ blocks, each weighing at least $1$; their total weight is $2n$. Prove that for every real number $r$ with $0\le r\le2n-2$ you can choose a subset of the blocks whose total weight is at least $r$ but at most $r+2$.
answer: Proof: sort the weights $x_1\le\dots\le x_n$; by induction the subset sums of $x_1,\dots,x_k$ have gaps at most $2$, because $x_k\le x_1+\dots+x_{k-1}+2$ (otherwise $2n>(n+1-k)(k+1)+k-1$, i.e. $n>k(n+1-k)$, which is false).

solutions.title: Subset sums have small gaps
solutions.body:
Let the weights be $x_1\le x_2\le\dots\le x_n$, and let $\sigma_k=x_1+\dots+x_k$. Let $S_k$ be the set of sums $\sum_{j\in J}x_j$ over subsets $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$. So $S_k$ is a finite set with minimum $0$ and maximum $\sigma_k$. Say a finite set has *mesh at most $2$* if any two consecutive elements, in increasing order, differ by at most $2$.

**Claim 1: $x_k\le\sigma_{k-1}+2$ for every $1\le k\le n$.** Suppose $x_k>\sigma_{k-1}+2$ for some $k$. Since all weights are at least $1$, $\sigma_{k-1}\ge k-1$, so $x_l\ge x_k>k+1$ for all $l\ge k$. Then
$$2n=\sigma_{k-1}+\sum_{l=k}^nx_l>(k-1)+(n-k+1)(k+1)=nk+n-k^2+k,$$
which gives $n>k(n+1-k)$. But $k(n+1-k)-n=(k-1)(n-k)\ge0$ for $1\le k\le n$, a contradiction.

**Claim 2: $S_k$ has mesh at most $2$ for every $k$.** Induction on $k$; $S_0=\{0\}$. For $k\ge1$,
$$S_k=S_{k-1}\cup(x_k+S_{k-1}),$$
the union of a mesh-$\le2$ set spanning $[0,\sigma_{k-1}]$ and its translate spanning $[x_k,x_k+\sigma_{k-1}]$. Let $u<w$ be consecutive elements of $S_k$ and suppose $w-u>2$. If $w\le\sigma_{k-1}$, then the largest element of $S_{k-1}$ that is $\le u$ and the smallest that is $\ge w$ are consecutive in $S_{k-1}$ and differ by more than $2$, which is impossible. So $w>\sigma_{k-1}$, and similarly $u<x_k$. But $\sigma_{k-1}$ and $x_k$ are elements of $S_k$, so $\sigma_{k-1}\le u$ and $w\le x_k$, giving $x_k-\sigma_{k-1}\ge w-u>2$. This contradicts Claim 1.

**Conclusion.** $S_n$ contains $0$ and $2n$ and has mesh at most $2$. Let $0\le r\le2n-2$, and let $s$ be the smallest element of $S_n$ with $s\ge r$; it exists because $2n\ge r$. If $s=0$ then $s=r\le r+2$. Otherwise the previous element $s'$ satisfies $s'<r$ and $s-s'\le2$, so $s<r+2$. Either way the blocks giving the sum $s$ weigh between $r$ and $r+2$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up on his desk, each showing heads or tails. He repeatedly does the following operation: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k>0$, then he flips the $k^{\text{th}}$ coin over; otherwise he stops the process. (For example, the process starting with $THT$ would be $THT\to HHT\to HTT\to TTT$, which takes three steps.)

Letting $C$ denote the initial configuration (a sequence of $n$ $H$'s and $T$'s), write $\ell(C)$ for the number of steps needed before all coins show $T$. Show that this number $\ell(C)$ is finite, and determine its average value over all $2^n$ possible initial configurations $C$.
answer: (a) Induction on $n$; (b) the average is $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{4}$.

prompt:
On a flat plane in Camelot, King Arthur builds a labyrinth $\mathfrak L$ consisting of $n$ walls, each of which is an infinite straight line. No two walls are parallel, and no three walls have a common point. Merlin then paints one side of each wall entirely red and the other side entirely blue.

At the intersection of two walls there are four corners: two diagonally opposite corners where a red side and a blue side meet, one corner where two red sides meet, and one corner where two blue sides meet. At each such intersection, there is a two-way door connecting the two diagonally opposite corners at which sides of different colours meet.

After Merlin paints the walls, Morgana then places some knights in the labyrinth. The knights can walk through doors, but cannot walk through walls.

Let $k(\mathfrak L)$ be the largest number $k$ such that, no matter how Merlin paints the labyrinth $\mathfrak L$, Morgana can always place at least $k$ knights such that no two of them can ever meet. For each $n$, what are all possible values for $k(\mathfrak L)$, where $\mathfrak L$ is a labyrinth with $n$ walls?

solutions.title: Count components; paint by compass direction
solutions.body:
Knights in the same region can meet, and knights can meet exactly when their regions are joined by a chain of doors. So, for a fixed painting, the largest number of knights that can never meet is the number of connected components of the graph $G$ whose vertices are the regions and whose edges are the doors. Hence $k(\mathfrak L)$ is the minimum of this number over all paintings.

**Counting regions.** $n$ walls in general position cut the plane into $\binom{n+1}2+1$ regions. This holds for $n=0$. The $n$-th wall meets the other $n-1$ walls at $n-1$ distinct points, so it passes through $n$ old regions and splits each into two, adding $n$ regions; and $\binom n2+1+n=\binom{n+1}2+1$.

**Lower bound: always at least $n+1$ components.** There are $\binom n2$ intersection points, so $G$ has $\binom n2$ edges. A graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges has at least $V-E$ components, because each edge lowers the number of components by at most one. So $G$ has at least $\binom{n+1}2+1-\binom n2=n+1$ components, whatever the painting.

**Upper bound: a painting with exactly $n+1$ components.** Choose coordinates so that no wall is horizontal or vertical. Merlin paints the west side of each wall red and the east side blue. Label each region by the number of walls it lies east of; labels are in $\{0,\dots,n\}$.

*Doors preserve labels.* At an intersection $V$ of walls $w_1,w_2$, the corner containing the direction due east is east of both walls, and the corner containing due west is west of both. These two corners are opposite each other. So the other two corners, namely the "south" corner between the two downward rays and the "north" corner between the two upward rays, are the red–blue corners, joined by the door. Each of them is east of one wall and west of the other, with the roles swapped. All other walls do not pass through $V$, so the two regions have the same label.

*Walking north.* Let a region $R$ with label $i$ be bounded above. Being a convex polygonal region, it attains its maximal height at a single vertex $V$, because no edge is horizontal. Near $V$, $R$ is the south corner, so the door at $V$ leads to the north corner, a region with the same label $i$ that reaches strictly higher than $V$. Repeating, the heights of the top vertices strictly increase. There are finitely many regions, so we end in a region with label $i$ that is unbounded above.

*Only one region per label is unbounded above.* Take a horizontal line $h$ above all intersection points. Every region unbounded above meets $h$, and $h$ crosses the $n$ walls at $n$ points, cutting $h$ into $n+1$ intervals lying in different regions. Going from west to east, each crossing moves from the west side to the east side of one wall, so the labels of these intervals are $0,1,\dots,n$, all different.

Hence every region with label $i$ is connected to the unique region with label $i$ that is unbounded above. So this painting has at most $n+1$ components, and by the lower bound exactly $n+1$.

Therefore $k(\mathfrak L)=n+1$ for every labyrinth with $n$ walls.

**Answer: the only possible value is $k(\mathfrak L)=n+1$.**

prompt:

answer: Proof: in graph language a move (toggle) preserves all degree parities; a connected graph that is not complete, not a cycle and not a tree has a toggle keeping it connected, so we reach a tree, and toggling a forest until stuck leaves a matching.

prompt: Let $n>1$ be an integer. Suppose we are given $2n$ points in a plane such that no three of them are collinear. The points are to be labelled $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_{2n}$ in some order. We then consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_1A_2A_3,\ \angle A_2A_3A_4,\ \dots,\ \angle A_{2n-2}A_{2n-1}A_{2n},\ \angle A_{2n-1}A_{2n}A_1,\ \angle A_{2n}A_1A_2$. We measure each angle in the way that gives the smallest positive value (i.e. between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Prove that there exists an ordering of the given points such that the resulting $2n$ angles can be separated into two groups with the sum of one group of angles equal to the sum of the other group.
answer: Proof: take a line $\ell$ with $n$ points on each side and let the cyclic order alternate between the sides. Rotate a line about $A_1,A_2,\dots$ in turn from $A_{i-1}A_i$ to $A_iA_{i+1}$ through the angle at $A_i$. It is never parallel to $\ell$, so the total signed rotation is $0$; group the angles by rotation direction.

solutions.title: A rotating line that never becomes parallel to $\ell$
solutions.body:
Choose a direction not parallel to any line through two of the points, and order the points by their projections onto a perpendicular line. A line $\ell$ in the chosen direction, placed between the $n$-th and $(n+1)$-th points, has $n$ points strictly on each side. Label the points so that $A_1,A_3,\dots,A_{2n-1}$ lie on one side and $A_2,A_4,\dots,A_{2n}$ on the other. Indices are taken mod $2n$. Then every segment $A_iA_{i+1}$ joins points on opposite sides of $\ell$. Let $\varphi_i=\angle A_{i-1}A_iA_{i+1}\in(0^\circ,180^\circ)$.

**Rotating at one vertex.** Let $m_i$ be the line through $A_i$ parallel to $\ell$. The points $A_{i-1}$ and $A_{i+1}$ are both on the other side of $\ell$ from $A_i$, hence both strictly on the same side of $m_i$. So the angle $\angle A_{i-1}A_iA_{i+1}$ lies, apart from its vertex, in one open half-plane bounded by $m_i$. Rotate the line $A_{i-1}A_i$ about $A_i$ through this angle, sweeping its ray $A_iA_{i-1}$ across the inside of the angle, until it becomes the line $A_iA_{i+1}$. The rotation is by exactly $\varphi_i$, clockwise or anticlockwise. During it the moving ray stays inside that open half-plane and the opposite ray inside the other one. So the moving line is never $m_i$, i.e. never parallel to $\ell$.

**The full tour.** Start with the line $s=A_{2n}A_1$ and do this successively at $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_{2n}$. After the step at $A_i$ the line is $A_iA_{i+1}$; after the last step it is $A_{2n}A_1$ again. Follow the direction angle $\theta(t)$ of $s$ continuously, as a real number. Each step changes $\theta$ by $\varepsilon_i\varphi_i$ with $\varepsilon_i=\pm1$, so the total change is $\Theta=\sum_i\varepsilon_i\varphi_i$. Since $s$ returns to the same line, $\Theta$ is a multiple of $180^\circ$. On the other hand, $s$ is never parallel to $\ell$, so $\theta(t)$ never takes a value $\theta_\ell+180^\circ k$. By continuity $\theta$ stays in one open interval of length $180^\circ$, so $|\Theta|<180^\circ$. Hence $\Theta=0$, i.e.
$$\sum_{\varepsilon_i=+1}\varphi_i=\sum_{\varepsilon_i=-1}\varphi_i .$$
These two groups (angles where $s$ turned anticlockwise and those where it turned clockwise) have equal sums. Both groups are nonempty, since all $\varphi_i>0$. ∎

prompt:
There are $60$ empty boxes $B_1,\dots,B_{60}$ in a row on a table and an unlimited supply of pebbles. Given a positive integer $n$, Alice and Bob play the following game.

In the first round, Alice takes $n$ pebbles and distributes them into the $60$ boxes as she wishes. Each subsequent round consists of two steps:

(a) Bob chooses an integer $k$ with $1\le k\le59$ and splits the boxes into the two groups $B_1,\dots,B_k$ and $B_{k+1},\dots,B_{60}$.

(b) Alice picks one of these two groups, adds one pebble to each box in that group, and removes one pebble from each box in the other group.

Bob wins if, at the end of any round, some box contains no pebbles. Find the smallest $n$ such that Alice can prevent Bob from winning.

solutions.title: V-shaped configurations and a ratchet for Bob
solutions.body:
Write $N=60$. A *$k$-move* is Bob's split into $B_1,\dots,B_k$ and $B_{k+1},\dots,B_{60}$. Let $L_k$ ("left") be the change in which $B_1,\dots,B_k$ gain a pebble and the rest lose one, and $R_k=-L_k$ ("right"). Configuration $X$ *dominates* $Y$ if $X$ has at least as many pebbles as $Y$ in every box.

For $1\le i\le60$ let $V_i$ be the "V-shaped" configuration with $1+|j-i|$ pebbles in box $B_j$. Then $V_{30}$ uses
$$60+(1+2+\dots+29)+(1+2+\dots+30)=60+435+465=960$$
pebbles.

**Alice wins with $960$ pebbles.** She starts with $V_{30}$. Suppose the current configuration $X$ dominates $V_i$ and Bob makes a $k$-move.

* If $k\ge i$, Alice picks the left group. Note that $V_{i+1}=V_i+1$ on boxes $j\le i$ and $V_i-1$ on boxes $j\ge i+1$. Boxes $j\le k$ get $X_j+1\ge V_i(j)+1\ge V_{i+1}(j)$, and boxes $j>k\ge i$ get $X_j-1\ge V_i(j)-1=V_{i+1}(j)$. So the new configuration dominates $V_{i+1}$; here $i+1\le k+1\le60$.
* If $k<i$, she symmetrically picks the right group, and the new configuration dominates $V_{i-1}$.

Every $V_i$ has at least one pebble in each box, so no box is ever empty.

**Bob wins against $n\le959$.**

*Key claim. If some $k\ge1$ and some $2k$ boxes $C_1<\dots<C_{2k}$ (in left-to-right order) each have at most $k$ pebbles, Bob can force a win.*

Let $p_1<p_2<\dots<p_k$ be the splits just after $C_k,C_{k+1},\dots,C_{2k-1}$; that is, $p_t$ separates $C_{k+t-1}$ from $C_{k+t}$. Bob first plays $p_1$. Suppose Alice picks left; the other case is the mirror image, with splits moving leftwards. Bob now follows a plan with stages, measured against fixed reference configurations $Z_0=Z$ (the configuration before his first move) and $Z_t=Z+L_{p_1}+\dots+L_{p_t}$. The invariant is: *at stage $t\ge1$ the current configuration is dominated by $Z_t$*, and at stage $t$ Bob plays $p_{t+1}$.

* If Alice picks left, the new configuration is dominated by $Z_t+L_{p_{t+1}}=Z_{t+1}$: go to stage $t+1$.
* If Alice picks right, it is dominated by $Z_t+R_{p_{t+1}}=Z_{t-1}+(L_{p_t}+R_{p_{t+1}})$. Since $p_t<p_{t+1}$, the vector $L_{p_t}+R_{p_{t+1}}$ is $-2$ on the boxes strictly between the two splits and $0$ elsewhere. So we drop to stage $t-1$, and the current configuration is dominated by $Z_{t-1}$ with at least $2$ pebbles to spare in total.

Let $D$ be the total of (reference configuration minus current configuration). A left pick keeps $D$, and a right pick increases it by at least $2$. While nobody has won, every box has at least one pebble, so $D\le\max_t\sum Z_t-60$ stays bounded, and right picks at stages $\ge1$ happen only finitely often. If stage $k$ is reached, box $C_{2k}$ lies to the right of all splits $p_1,\dots,p_k$, so it holds at most $Z(C_{2k})-k\le0$ pebbles, and Bob has won.

The remaining possibility is a right pick at stage $1$, which drops to stage $0$. Then the current configuration $Z'$ is dominated by $Z$ and has strictly fewer pebbles in total. In particular, the same $2k$ boxes still hold at most $k$ pebbles each. Bob restarts the whole procedure from $Z'$. Each restart strictly lowers the total number of pebbles, so there are only finitely many restarts, and eventually Bob wins.

*Using the claim.* Suppose $n\le959$. If Alice leaves a box empty in round 1, Bob wins at once. Otherwise every box has at least $1$ pebble. If for some $k\in\{1,\dots,30\}$ at least $2k$ boxes had at most $k$ pebbles, Bob would win by the claim. If not, then for each $k=1,\dots,30$ at least $60-(2k-1)=61-2k$ boxes have at least $k+1$ pebbles. Since the total equals $\sum_{k\ge0}\#\{\text{boxes with}\ge k+1\text{ pebbles}\}$,
$$n\ \ge\ 60+\sum_{k=1}^{30}(61-2k)=60+1830-930=960,$$
a contradiction.

**Answer: 960.**

prompt:
Alice has a map of Wonderland, a country consisting of $n\ge2$ towns. For every pair of towns, there is a narrow road going from one town to the other. One day, all the roads are declared to be "one way" only. Alice has no information on the direction of the roads, but the King of Hearts has offered to help her. She is allowed to ask him a number of questions. For each question in turn, Alice chooses a pair of towns and the King of Hearts tells her the direction of the road connecting those two towns.

Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one outgoing road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.
answer: Proof: build a spanning tree in which every town but one ($T$) has a known outgoing road ($n-1$ questions); ask $T$'s roads until two outgoing ones appear; then repeatedly ask about unknown pairs among the towns not yet known to have two outgoing roads (each answer eliminates one town) until at most $2$ remain, and check those directly. This takes at most $4n-7$ questions in total.

solutions.title: Eliminate towns one question at a time
solutions.body:
Think of a tournament on $n$ vertices. Let $S$ be the set of towns not yet known to have at least two outgoing roads; initially $|S|=n$. Alice is done once $S=\varnothing$ (answer "no") or once some town in $S$ has all its roads known (then she knows its out-degree). Whenever every remaining town in $S$ has all roads known, she knows the answer. We show she needs at most $4n-7<4n$ questions.

**Phase 1** (1 question). Ask about two towns; say the road goes $A\to B$. Put $T=B$.

**Phase 2** ($n-2$ questions). Throughout, $T$ has a known incoming road and no known outgoing road. For each of the other $n-2$ towns $X$ in turn, ask about $X$–$T$. If $X\to T$, keep $T$; now $X$ has one known outgoing road. If $T\to X$, the old $T$ now has one known outgoing road and $X$ becomes the new $T$.

After $n-1$ questions, the known roads form a spanning tree: each question joined a new town to the tree. The final $T$ has no known outgoing road, and every other town has **exactly one** known outgoing road.

**Phase 3.** Ask about every road from $T$ not yet known, stopping as soon as two outgoing roads from $T$ are found. If this never happens, all roads at $T$ are known and $T$ has at most one outgoing road: answer "yes" after at most $(n-1)+(n-2)=2n-3$ questions. Otherwise, suppose it took $k$ questions. At least one road at $T$ was known already, so $2\le k\le n-2$, and in particular $n\ge4$. The $k-2$ towns $X$ with $X\to T$ now have two known outgoing roads, and the last question did the same for $T$; remove them all from $S$. Then $|S|=n-k+1\ge3$ after $n-1+k$ questions. Every town in $S$ still has exactly one known outgoing road. The known roads inside $S$ form a forest, since this phase only asked roads at $T\notin S$.

**Phase 4.** While $S$ contains a pair with unknown road, ask about it. One of the two gets a second known outgoing road and leaves $S$; the other only gains an incoming road. So the invariants hold: each town of $S$ has exactly one known outgoing road, and the known roads inside $S$ form a forest. If $|S|=s\ge3$, a forest on $s$ vertices has at most $s-1<\binom s2$ edges, so an unknown pair exists. Hence the phase ends with $t\in\{1,2\}$ towns in $S$, after $n-k+1-t$ more questions: $2n-t$ in total.

**Phase 5.** Ask about every unknown road at the remaining towns of $S$. Then Alice knows the out-degree of every town in $S$, and all other towns have at least two outgoing roads, so she knows the answer. The original tree is connected and spans all $n$ towns.

* If $t=1$, the remaining town has $n-1$ roads, at least one known from the tree: at most $n-2$ questions, total at most $3n-3\le4n-7$ as $n\ge4$.
* If $t=2$, the road between the two towns is already known. Among the $2(n-2)$ roads from them to other towns, at least one is a tree edge, since the tree is connected and $n>2$. So there are at most $2n-5$ questions, total at most $(2n-2)+(2n-5)=4n-7$.

In all cases Alice uses at most $4n-7<4n$ questions. ∎

prompt:
For any two different real numbers $x$ and $y$, we define $D(x,y)$ to be the unique integer $d$ satisfying $2^d\le|x-y|<2^{d+1}$. Given a set of reals $\mathcal F$, and an element $x\in\mathcal F$, we say that the *scales* of $x$ in $\mathcal F$ are the values of $D(x,y)$ for $y\in\mathcal F$ with $x\ne y$.

Let $k$ be a given positive integer. Suppose that each member $x$ of $\mathcal F$ has at most $k$ different scales in $\mathcal F$ (note that these scales may depend on $x$). What is the maximum possible size of $\mathcal F$?

solutions.title: A weighted count that never exceeds 1
solutions.body:
**Construction.** $\mathcal F=\{0,1,2,\dots,2^k-1\}$ works: every difference lies in $[1,2^k-1]$, so all scales are in $\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}$.

**Upper bound.** For a finite set $\mathcal S$ and $x\in\mathcal S$, let $r_{\mathcal S}(x)$ be the number of different scales of $x$ in $\mathcal S$.

**Lemma.** For every finite nonempty $\mathcal S$, $\displaystyle w(\mathcal S)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal S}2^{-r_{\mathcal S}(x)}\le1$.

*Proof.* Induction on $|\mathcal S|$. If $\mathcal S=\{x\}$ then $w=2^0=1$. Let $|\mathcal S|\ge2$ with smallest element $x_1$ and largest $x_n$. The largest distance in $\mathcal S$ is $x_n-x_1$, so $d=D(x_1,x_n)$ is the largest scale occurring in $\mathcal S$. Put
$$O=\{x\in\mathcal S: D(x,x_n)=d\},\qquad E=\{x\in\mathcal S:D(x_1,x)=d\},\qquad R=\mathcal S\setminus(O\cup E).$$
$O\ni x_1$ and $E\ni x_n$ are nonempty. They are disjoint: for $x\in O\cap E$ we would get $x_n-x_1=(x-x_1)+(x_n-x)\ge2^d+2^d=2^{d+1}$, contradicting $D(x_1,x_n)=d$.

*For $x\in O$, every $y$ with $D(x,y)=d$ lies in $E$.* If $y<x$ then $|y-x_n|>|x-x_n|\ge2^d$ and $|y-x|\ge2^d$, so $|y-x_n|\ge2^{d+1}$, which is impossible. So $y>x\ge x_1$ and $|y-x_1|\ge|y-x|\ge2^d$, which forces $D(x_1,y)=d$, i.e. $y\in E$. Symmetrically, for $x\in E$ all partners at scale $d$ lie in $O$.

Let $\mathcal S_O=\mathcal S\setminus E=O\cup R$ and $\mathcal S_E=\mathcal S\setminus O=E\cup R$, both smaller than $\mathcal S$. Removing elements never creates new scales, so $r_{\mathcal S_O}(x)\le r_{\mathcal S}(x)$ and $r_{\mathcal S_E}(x)\le r_{\mathcal S}(x)$ for $x\in R$. For $x\in O$, the scale $d$ occurs in $\mathcal S$ (with $x_n$) but not in $\mathcal S_O$, so $r_{\mathcal S_O}(x)\le r_{\mathcal S}(x)-1$; similarly $r_{\mathcal S_E}(x)\le r_{\mathcal S}(x)-1$ for $x\in E$. Therefore
$$w(\mathcal S)=\sum_{R}2^{-r_{\mathcal S}}+\sum_O2^{-r_{\mathcal S}}+\sum_E2^{-r_{\mathcal S}}
\le\tfrac12\sum_R\big(2^{-r_{\mathcal S_O}}+2^{-r_{\mathcal S_E}}\big)+\tfrac12\sum_O2^{-r_{\mathcal S_O}}+\tfrac12\sum_E2^{-r_{\mathcal S_E}}$$
$$=\tfrac12\big(w(\mathcal S_O)+w(\mathcal S_E)\big)\le1$$
by the induction hypothesis. $\square$

**Conclusion.** If $\mathcal F$ had more than $2^k$ elements, take a subset $\mathcal S$ of exactly $2^k+1$ of them. Each $x\in\mathcal S$ has $r_{\mathcal S}(x)\le k$, so $w(\mathcal S)\ge(2^k+1)2^{-k}>1$, contradicting the lemma.

**Answer: the maximum size is $2^k$.**

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Circle $\Gamma$ passes through $A$, meets segments $AB$ and $AC$ again at points $D$ and $E$ respectively, and intersects segment $BC$ at $F$ and $G$ such that $F$ lies between $B$ and $G$. The tangent to circle $BDF$ at $F$ and the tangent to circle $CEG$ at $G$ meet at point $T$. Suppose that points $A$ and $T$ are distinct. Prove that line $AT$ is parallel to $BC$.
answer: Proof: tangent–chord and the cyclic quadrilateral $ADFG$ give $\angle(FT,BC)=\angle(BC,GA)$, and similarly $\angle(GT,BC)=\angle(BC,FA)$. So the reflection in the perpendicular bisector of $FG$ maps lines $GA,FA$ to $FT,GT$, hence $A$ to $T$, and $AT\parallel BC$.

solutions.title: A reflection swapping $F$ and $G$
solutions.body:
Write $\measuredangle(m,n)$ for the directed angle from line $m$ to line $n$, modulo $180^\circ$.

By the tangent–chord angle in circle $BDF$, then the collinearity of $A,D,B$, then the cyclic quadrilateral $ADFG$ on $\Gamma$:
$$\measuredangle(FT,BC)=\measuredangle(FT,FB)=\measuredangle(DF,DB)=\measuredangle(DF,DA)=\measuredangle(GF,GA)=\measuredangle(BC,GA).$$
In the same way, using circle $CEG$, the collinearity of $A,E,C$ and the cyclic quadrilateral $AEGF$:
$$\measuredangle(GT,BC)=\measuredangle(GT,GC)=\measuredangle(EG,EC)=\measuredangle(EG,EA)=\measuredangle(FG,FA)=\measuredangle(BC,FA).$$

Let $\sigma$ be the reflection in the perpendicular bisector of $FG$. It swaps $F$ and $G$, fixes the direction of $BC$, and reverses directed angles, so $\measuredangle(BC,\sigma(m))=-\measuredangle(BC,m)$ for every line $m$. Thus $\sigma(GA)$ is the line through $F$ with $\measuredangle(BC,\sigma(GA))=-\measuredangle(BC,GA)=-\measuredangle(FT,BC)=\measuredangle(BC,FT)$ (first display), i.e. $\sigma(GA)=FT$. Likewise, by the second display, $\sigma(FA)=GT$.

Lines $GA$ and $FA$ are distinct ($A\notin BC$) and meet only at $A$. Hence $T=FT\cap GT=\sigma(GA)\cap\sigma(FA)=\sigma(A)$. A point and its image under $\sigma$ lie on a line perpendicular to the axis of $\sigma$, that is, parallel to $BC$. Since $A\ne T$, line $AT$ is parallel to $BC$. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Denote by $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, and let these circles be tangent to segments $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Let line $MN$ meet circles $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ again at $P\ne M$ and $Q\ne N$, respectively. Prove that $MP=NQ$.
answer: Proof: the right triangles $DMO_B$ and $DNO_C$ are similar (both angles at $D$ equal $\frac12\angle A$), so $\frac{DN}{DM}=\frac{r_C}{r_B}$; chord lengths give $MP=2r_B\sin\angle DMN$, $NQ=2r_C\sin\angle MND$, and the sine rule in $DMN$ finishes.

solutions.title: Similar right triangles and the sine rule
solutions.body:
Let $O_B,O_C$ be the centres and $r_B,r_C$ the radii of $\omega_B,\omega_C$.

**Similar right triangles.** Since $AFDC$ and $ABDE$ are cyclic (right angles at $F,D$ and at $E,D$), $\angle FDB=\angle BAC=\angle CDE$. The incentre $O_B$ of $BDF$ lies on the bisector of $\angle FDB$, so $\angle MDO_B=\frac12\angle FDB=\frac12\angle BAC$; similarly $\angle NDO_C=\frac12\angle BAC$. The triangles $DMO_B$ and $DNO_C$ have right angles at $M$ and $N$, so they are similar, and
$$\frac{DN}{DM}=\frac{O_CN}{O_BM}=\frac{r_C}{r_B}.$$

**Chord lengths.** Let $\varphi=\angle DMN$ and $\psi=\angle MND$. Line $DF$ is tangent to $\omega_B$ at $M$, and the chord $MP$ lies on line $MN$. By the tangent–chord angle, the chord $MP$ subtends an inscribed angle equal to the angle between the tangent $DF$ and the line $MN$, which is $\varphi$ or $180^\circ-\varphi$. Either way,
$$MP=2r_B\sin\varphi,\qquad\text{and likewise}\qquad NQ=2r_C\sin\psi.$$

**Sine rule** in triangle $DMN$: $\dfrac{DN}{DM}=\dfrac{\sin\varphi}{\sin\psi}$.

Therefore
$$\frac{MP}{NQ}=\frac{r_B}{r_C}\cdot\frac{\sin\varphi}{\sin\psi}=\frac{DM}{DN}\cdot\frac{DN}{DM}=1,$$
so $MP=NQ$. ∎

prompt: In triangle $ABC$, let $A_1$ and $B_1$ be two points on sides $BC$ and $AC$, and let $P$ and $Q$ be two points on segments $AA_1$ and $BB_1$, respectively, so that line $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$. On ray $PB_1$, beyond $B_1$, let $P_1$ be a point so that $\angle PP_1C=\angle BAC$. Similarly, on ray $QA_1$, beyond $A_1$, let $Q_1$ be a point so that $\angle CQ_1Q=\angle CBA$. Show that points $P$, $Q$, $P_1$, and $Q_1$ are concyclic.
answer: Proof: let $AA_1$, $BB_1$ meet the circumcircle again at $A_2$, $B_2$; Reim gives $P,Q,A_2,B_2$ concyclic, and angle chases show $Q_1$ and $P_1$ lie on the same circle.

prompt: Let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$. Let $AP$ meet $BC$ at $A_1$, let $BP$ meet $CA$ at $B_1$, and let $CP$ meet $AB$ at $C_1$. Let $A_2$ be the point such that $A_1$ is the midpoint of $PA_2$, let $B_2$ be the point such that $B_1$ is the midpoint of $PB_2$, and let $C_2$ be the point such that $C_1$ is the midpoint of $PC_2$. Prove that points $A_2$, $B_2$, and $C_2$ cannot all lie strictly inside the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.
answer: Proof: put the circumcentre at the origin with radius $1$ and $P=\alpha A+\beta B+\gamma C$ ($\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$, sum $1$). Then $A_2=\frac{(1+\alpha)P-2\alpha A}{1-\alpha}$, and $\sum\frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2(1+\alpha)}|A_2|^2=\sum\frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2(1+\alpha)}$, so some $|A_2|,|B_2|,|C_2|$ is at least $1$.

solutions.title: Vectors from the circumcentre
solutions.body:
Place the circumcentre at the origin and take the circumradius as $1$, so $|A|^2=|B|^2=|C|^2=1$ for the position vectors. A point strictly inside the circumcircle has $|X|<1$.

Since $P$ is inside the triangle, $P=\alpha A+\beta B+\gamma C$ with $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$ and $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$. The point $A_1$ is where line $AP$ meets $BC$:
$$A_1=\frac{\beta B+\gamma C}{\beta+\gamma}=\frac{P-\alpha A}{1-\alpha},\qquad A_2=2A_1-P=\frac{(1+\alpha)P-2\alpha A}{1-\alpha}.$$
Hence, using $|A|^2=1$,
$$(1-\alpha)^2|A_2|^2=(1+\alpha)^2|P|^2-4\alpha(1+\alpha)\,A\cdot P+4\alpha^2,$$
$$\frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2(1+\alpha)}|A_2|^2=\frac{1+\alpha}2|P|^2-2\alpha\,A\cdot P+\frac{2\alpha^2}{1+\alpha}.\tag{1}$$
The same holds for $B_2$ with $\beta,B$ and for $C_2$ with $\gamma,C$. Add the three identities. On the right:
* $\frac{(1+\alpha)+(1+\beta)+(1+\gamma)}2|P|^2=2|P|^2$;
* $-2(\alpha A+\beta B+\gamma C)\cdot P=-2|P|^2$;
* and $\dfrac{2\alpha^2}{1+\alpha}=\dfrac{3\alpha-1}2+\dfrac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2(1+\alpha)}$. To check this, multiply by $2(1+\alpha)$: $(3\alpha-1)(1+\alpha)+(1-\alpha)^2=4\alpha^2$. Moreover $\sum\frac{3\alpha-1}2=\frac{3-3}2=0$.

So, with the positive weights $w_\alpha=\frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2(1+\alpha)}$ and similarly $w_\beta,w_\gamma$,
$$w_\alpha|A_2|^2+w_\beta|B_2|^2+w_\gamma|C_2|^2=w_\alpha+w_\beta+w_\gamma .$$
If all three of $|A_2|,|B_2|,|C_2|$ were less than $1$, the left side would be smaller than the right side. Hence at least one of $A_2,B_2,C_2$ is not strictly inside the circumcircle. ∎

prompt: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD=DE$ and $\angle EDC\ne2\cdot\angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP=AE$ and $BP=BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD)+\operatorname{area}(ADE)=\operatorname{area}(ABD)+\operatorname{area}(ABP)$.
answer: Proof: $f(X)=[BCX]+[AXE]-[ABX]-[ABP]$ is affine, and the area condition is $f(D)=0$ with $D$ on the perpendicular bisector $\ell$ of $CE$. If $P\in CE$, a coordinate check shows $f\equiv0$ on $\ell$. If not, $f$ vanishes on $\ell$ only at the circumcentre $O$ of $CEP'$ ($P'$ the reflection of $P$ in $AB$) and $f(T)=-2[ABP]\neq0$ at the circumcentre $T$ of $CEP$. Finally, $O=D$ would force $\angle EDC=2\angle ADB$.

solutions.title: A linear function along the perpendicular bisector of $CE$
solutions.body:
Use signed areas $[XYZ]$, positive for counterclockwise triangles, with $ABCDE$ labelled counterclockwise. Write $u\times v=u_1v_2-u_2v_1$, so $[XYZ]=\frac12(Y-X)\times(Z-X)$. Define, for every point $X$,
$$f(X)=[BCX]+[AXE]-[ABX]-[ABP].$$
The triangles $BCD$, $ADE$, $ABD$, $ABP$ are all counterclockwise, so the area condition is exactly $f(D)=0$. Let $\ell$ be the perpendicular bisector of $CE$; $D\in\ell$ because $CD=DE$. The function $f$ is affine.

**Step 1 (when is $f$ constant on $\ell$?).** The linear part of $f$ is $X\mapsto\frac12W\times X$ with
$$W=(C-B)+(A-E)-(B-A)=(C-E)-2(B-A).$$
Along $\ell$ (direction $u\perp C-E$), $f$ is constant iff $W\times u=0$, i.e. iff $W\cdot(C-E)=0$. With $U=C-B$, $V=E-A$, $G=B-A$ we have $C-E=U-V+G$ and $W=U-V-G$, so $W\cdot(C-E)=|U-V|^2-|G|^2$. Thus
$$f\text{ is constant on }\ell\iff|(C-B)-(E-A)|=|B-A|.\tag{*}$$

**Step 2: if $P\in CE$, the area condition holds.** As $P$ is interior, it lies strictly between $C$ and $E$. Take $P$ as origin and $CE$ as the $x$-axis: $E=(e,0)$, $C=(c,0)$, $A=(a_1,a_2)$, $B=(b_1,b_2)$. Then $AE=AP$ gives $(e-a_1)^2=a_1^2$, so $e=2a_1$; similarly $c=2b_1$. Now $E-A=(a_1,-a_2)$ and $C-B=(b_1,-b_2)$, so $|(C-B)-(E-A)|=|B-A|$, and by $(*)$, $f$ is constant on $\ell$.

The point $Q=A+B$ has $x$-coordinate $a_1+b_1=\frac{e+c}2$, so $Q\in\ell$. Also $[ABQ]=\frac12(B-A)\times B=-\frac12A\times B=-[ABP]$. Hence
$$f(Q)=[BCQ]+[AQE]=\tfrac12\big((C-B)\times A+B\times(E-A)\big)=\tfrac12\big(C\times A+B\times E-2B\times A\big).$$
With $C=(2b_1,0)$ and $E=(2a_1,0)$ this is $\frac12\big(2b_1a_2-2a_1b_2-2(b_1a_2-b_2a_1)\big)=0$. So $f\equiv0$ on $\ell$, in particular $f(D)=0$.

**Step 3: a reflection identity.** *Let $Y$ satisfy $AY=AE$, $BY=BC$, $Y\notin CE$, and let $Z$ be the circumcentre of $CEY$ (so $Z\in\ell$). Then $f(Z)=-[ABY]-[ABP]$.* The reflection in the perpendicular bisector of $EY$ fixes $A$ and $Z$ and swaps $E,Y$, and it reverses orientation, so $[AZE]=-[AZY]$; similarly $[BCZ]=-[BYZ]$. Thus
$$[BCZ]+[AZE]=[YBZ]+[YZA]=[YBZA]=[BZA]+[BAY]=[ABZ]-[ABY],$$
where $[YBZA]$ is the signed area of the quadrilateral, split along either diagonal. Substituting gives the claim.

**Step 4: if $P\notin CE$, the area condition fails.** Let $P'$ be the reflection of $P$ in $AB$; then $AP'=AE$, $BP'=BC$, and $[ABP']=-[ABP]$.

*Lemma A: $P'\notin CE$.* $P$ lies strictly on the inner side of line $AB$, like $C$ and $E$, so $P'$ is strictly on the other side and not on segment $CE$. Suppose $P'$ is on line $CE$. The statement is symmetric under $(A,B,C,D,E)\to(B,A,E,D,C)$, so we may assume $C$ lies strictly between $E$ and $P'$. Measure directions at $B$, reflecting the picture if needed, with ray $BC$ at $0^\circ$ and ray $BA$ at $\beta=\angle ABC\in(0^\circ,180^\circ)$. As $P$ is inside angle $ABC$, ray $BP$ has direction $\varphi\in(0,\beta)$, so ray $BP'$ has direction $\psi=2\beta-\varphi\in(\beta,2\beta)$. Scale so that $BC=1$, with $B$ at the origin. Then $C=(1,0)$ and $P'=(\cos\psi,\sin\psi)$; also $E=C+s(C-P')$ with $s>0$, and $A=r(\cos\beta,\sin\beta)$ with $r>0$. A short computation gives $P'-E=(1+s)(P'-C)$ and $|E|^2=1+2s(1+s)(1-\cos\psi)$. So $AE=AP'$, i.e. $2A\cdot(P'-E)=|P'|^2-|E|^2$, becomes
$$A\cdot(P'-C)=-s(1-\cos\psi)<0 .$$
But $A\cdot(P'-C)=r\big(\cos(\psi-\beta)-\cos\beta\big)>0$, because $0<\psi-\beta<\beta<180^\circ$. Contradiction.

*Lemma B: the circumcentre $O$ of $CEP'$ is not $D$.* If $O=D$ then $DE=DP'=DC$. So the perpendicular bisector of $EP'$ is line $DA$ and that of $P'C$ is line $DB$. Reflecting in $DA$ and then in $DB$ maps $E\mapsto P'\mapsto C$; this composition is the rotation about $D$ by twice the angle from $DA$ to $DB$. By convexity, the rays $DE,DA,DB,DC$ occur in this order inside the angle $EDC<180^\circ$. So rotating by $2\angle ADB$ takes ray $DE$ to ray $DC$, i.e. $\angle EDC\equiv2\angle ADB\pmod{360^\circ}$. Both angles lie in $(0^\circ,360^\circ)$, so $\angle EDC=2\angle ADB$, which is excluded.

Now apply Step 3 twice. With $Y=P$ and $T$ the circumcentre of $CEP$: $f(T)=-2[ABP]\ne0$. With $Y=P'$, allowed by Lemma A: $f(O)=[ABP]-[ABP]=0$. Hence $f$ is not constant on $\ell$, and its only zero on $\ell$ is $O$. By Lemma B, $D\ne O$, so $f(D)\ne0$ and the area condition fails.

Steps 2 and 4 together prove the equivalence. ∎

prompt: Let $I$ be the incentre of acute-angled triangle $ABC$. Let the incircle meet $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Let line $EF$ intersect the circumcircle of the triangle at $P$ and $Q$, such that $F$ lies between $E$ and $P$. Prove that $\angle DPA+\angle AQD=\angle QIP$.
answer: Proof: the spiral similarity $\varphi$ taking kite $AFIE$ to kite $NBMC$ ($N,M$ the arc midpoints of $BC$) maps $P,Q$ to $P'=NP\cap BC$, $Q'=NQ\cap BC$; with $L$ the midpoint of $BC$, the points $P,Q,D,L$ are concyclic (harmonic division), and $MLPP'$, $MLQQ'$ are cyclic. An angle chase gives $\angle DPA+\angle AQD=\angle P'MQ'=\angle PIQ$.

solutions.title: A spiral similarity onto the arc midpoints
solutions.body:
Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle. Let $N$ and $M$ be the midpoints of the arcs $BC$ containing and not containing $A$, and let $L$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Then $NM$ is a diameter of $\Gamma$, perpendicular to $BC$ at $L$, and $M$ lies on $AI$. We argue in the standard configuration: $P$ lies on arc $AB$ and $Q$ on arc $AC$ (the arcs not containing the third vertex), and $P',Q'$ below lie on opposite sides of $L$. Other configurations go the same way with directed angles.

**1. The spiral similarity.** $AFIE$ is a kite with right angles at $F,E$ and apex angle $\angle FAE=\angle BAC$. $NBMC$ is a kite with right angles at $B,C$, since $NM$ is a diameter, and apex angle $\angle BNC=\angle BAC$. Both have the same orientation, because $A$ and $N$ are on the same side of $BC$. So there is a direct similarity $\varphi$ with $A\mapsto N$, $F\mapsto B$, $I\mapsto M$, $E\mapsto C$. It turns every line through the same directed angle $\measuredangle(AB,NB)$.

Since $A,N,P,B$ are concyclic, $\measuredangle(PA,PN)=\measuredangle(BA,BN)$. So $\varphi$ maps line $AP$ to the line through $N$ obtained by turning $AP$ through that angle, namely line $NP$. Similarly $\varphi(AQ)=NQ$, and $\varphi(EF)=CB$. Hence
$$\varphi(P)=P':=NP\cap BC,\qquad\varphi(Q)=Q':=NQ\cap BC,\qquad\varphi(I)=M,$$
and in particular $\angle PIQ=\angle P'MQ'$.

**2. $P,Q,D,L$ are concyclic.** If $AB=AC$ then $D=L$ and nothing is needed below. Otherwise let $Z=EF\cap BC$. Menelaus for triangle $ABC$ and line $EFZ$, with $AF=AE$, $BF=BD$, $CE=CD$, gives
$$\frac{ZB}{ZC}=\frac{FB}{FA}\cdot\frac{EA}{EC}=\frac{BD}{CD},$$
so $(B,C;D,Z)$ is harmonic. With coordinates $L=0$, $B=-m$, $C=m$, $D=d$, $Z=z$ on line $BC$, this reads $\frac{m+d}{m-d}=\frac{z+m}{z-m}$, i.e. $dz=m^2$. Hence
$$ZB\cdot ZC=z^2-m^2=z(z-d)=ZL\cdot ZD .$$
Also $ZB\cdot ZC=ZP\cdot ZQ$ (power of $Z$ with respect to $\Gamma$), so $ZP\cdot ZQ=ZD\cdot ZL$ and $P,Q,D,L$ are concyclic. $D$ and $L$ lie on the same side of line $PQ$, because $Z$ is outside segment $BC$. So $\angle QDP=\angle QLP$.

**3. Two more circles.** $\angle MPN=90^\circ$ (diameter) and $P'\in NP$, so $\angle MPP'=90^\circ$; also $\angle MLP'=90^\circ$. Hence $M,L,P,P'$ lie on the circle with diameter $MP'$; similarly for $M,L,Q,Q'$. Here $P$ is above $BC$ and $M$ below, and $P$ lies between $N$ and $P'$. So $\angle LPN=180^\circ-\angle LPP'=\angle LMP'$, and likewise $\angle NQL=\angle LMQ'$.

**4. $A$ and $N$ are on the same side of $EF$.** $EF\perp AM$, and $\angle NAM=90^\circ$, so $N$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $EF$. Hence $\angle PAQ=\angle PNQ$.

**5. The angle chase.** The quadrilateral $APDQ$ is convex: its diagonals $AD$ and $PQ$ cross, since $AD$ crosses segment $EF$. The quadrilateral $NPLQ$ is convex: segment $NL$ lies on the diameter and crosses chord $PQ$. Therefore
$$\angle DPA+\angle AQD=360^\circ-\angle PAQ-\angle QDP=360^\circ-\angle PNQ-\angle QLP=\angle LPN+\angle NQL$$
$$=\angle LMP'+\angle LMQ'=\angle P'MQ'=\angle PIQ .$$
∎

prompt:
Find all pairs $(m,n)$ of positive integers satisfying the equation
$$(2^n-1)(2^n-2)(2^n-4)\cdots(2^n-2^{n-1})=m!$$
Find all triples $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers such that $a^3+b^3+c^3=(abc)^2$.
answer: $(a,b,c)=(1,2,3)$ and its permutations (six triples).

solutions.title: Bound $c$, then $b$, then check
solutions.body:
The equation is symmetric, so assume $a\ge b\ge c$.

**$c=1$.** We have $3a^3\ge a^3+b^3+c^3=(abc)^2>a^3$, so $3a\ge b^2c^2>a$. In particular $b^2c^2-a$ is a positive integer, and
$$b^3+c^3=a^2(b^2c^2-a)\ge a^2 .$$
Hence $18b^3\ge9(b^3+c^3)\ge9a^2\ge(b^2c^2)^2=b^4c^4\ge b^3c^5$, using $b\ge c$ at the end. So $c^5\le18$, i.e. $c=1$.

**$b\le4$.** Now $a^3+b^3+1=a^2b^2$. If $a=b$ this gives $2b^3+1=b^4$, i.e. $b^3(b-2)=1$, impossible. So $a\ge b+1$ and $a^3-b^3\ge3b^2+3b+1>1$. Therefore
$$a^3<a^3+b^3+1=a^2b^2<2a^3,$$
so $a<b^2<2a$. Then
$$4(1+b^3)=4a^2(b^2-a)\ge4a^2>b^4,$$
so $b^3(b-4)<4$, giving $b\le4$. Also $b\ge2$, because $b=1$ would give $a<1$.

**Cases**, with $\frac{b^2}2<a<b^2$:
* $b=2$: $a^3-4a^2+9=0$ with $a=3$: $27-36+9=0$. ✓
* $b=3$: $a^3-9a^2+28=a^2(a-9)+28$ with $5\le a\le8$: this is at most $-a^2+28<0$. No solution.
* $b=4$: $a^3-16a^2+65=a^2(a-16)+65$ with $9\le a\le15$: at most $-a^2+65<0$. No solution.

So $(a,b,c)=(3,2,1)$, and indeed $27+8+1=36=6^2$.

**Answer: $(1,2,3)$ and all its permutations.**

prompt: We say that a set $S$ of integers is *rootiful* if, for any positive integer $n$ and any $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n\in S$, all integer roots of the polynomial $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$ are also in $S$. Find all rootiful sets of integers that contain all numbers of the form $2^a-2^b$ for positive integers $a$ and $b$.
answer: Only $S=\mathbb Z$. Every $n$ has a multiple $2^{\alpha+1}(2^{\varphi(t)}-1)\in S$ (with $n=2^\alpha t$, $t$ odd), and writing a multiple $N$ of $n$ in base $n$ makes $n$ a root of $a_kx^k+\dots+a_1x-N$ with digits in $S$, giving induction.

solutions.title: Base-$n$ digits as coefficients
solutions.body:
$\mathbb Z$ itself is clearly rootiful. Let $S$ be rootiful and contain all $2^a-2^b$; we show $S=\mathbb Z$.

**Small elements.** $0=2^1-2^1$, $2=2^2-2^1$ and $-2=2^1-2^2$ are in $S$. Hence $-1\in S$ (root of $2x+2$) and $1\in S$ (root of $2x-2$). If $m\in S$ then $-m\in S$, as the root of $x+m$ (coefficients $1,m\in S$). So it suffices to show that every positive integer is in $S$.

**Every $n\ge1$ has a positive multiple in $S$.** Write $n=2^\alpha t$ with $t$ odd. By Euler's theorem $t\mid2^{\varphi(t)}-1$, so
$$n\ \big|\ 2^{\alpha+1}\big(2^{\varphi(t)}-1\big)=2^{\alpha+\varphi(t)+1}-2^{\alpha+1}\in S,$$
and this number is positive.

**Induction.** Suppose $0,1,\dots,n-1\in S$ for some $n\ge2$. Let $N>0$ be a multiple of $n$ in $S$, and write it in base $n$:
$$N=a_kn^k+a_{k-1}n^{k-1}+\dots+a_1n+a_0,\qquad0\le a_i\le n-1,\ k\ge1 .$$
Since $n\mid N$, $a_0=0$. All digits $a_i$ are in $S$ by the induction hypothesis, and $-N\in S$. Thus $n$ is an integer root of
$$a_kx^k+\dots+a_1x+(-N),$$
whose coefficients lie in $S$, so $n\in S$. This completes the induction.

**Answer: the only such set is $S=\mathbb Z$.**

prompt:
Let $\mathbb Z_{>0}$ be the set of positive integers. A positive integer constant $C$ is given. Find all functions $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ such that, for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ satisfying $a+b>C$,
$$a+f(b)\mid a^2+b\,f(a).$$
answer: $f(a)=ka$ for a positive integer constant $k$ (for every $C$). Show $b\mid f(b)^2$, so $f(p)=k(p)\,p$ with $k(p)\le f(1)$; some $k$ occurs for infinitely many primes $p$, and then $a+kp\mid f(a)-ka$ forces $f(a)=ka$.

solutions.title: Primes force linearity
solutions.body:
**These work.** If $f(a)=ka$ then $a^2+bf(a)=a(a+kb)=a\big(a+f(b)\big)$.

**Conversely**, let $f$ satisfy the condition.

*Upper bound.* With $a=1$ and $b\ge C$: $1+f(b)\mid1+bf(1)$, so $f(b)\le bf(1)$.

*$b\mid f(b)^2$ for every $b$.* Choose $n$ so large that $a=nb-f(b)\ge1$ and $a+b>C$. Then $a+f(b)=nb$ divides $a^2+bf(a)$, hence $b\mid a^2+bf(a)$, so $b\mid a^2=(nb-f(b))^2$, i.e. $b\mid f(b)^2$.

In particular $p\mid f(p)$ for every prime $p$. Write $f(p)=k(p)\,p$. For $p\ge C$ we have $1\le k(p)\le f(1)$, so some value $k$ equals $k(p)$ for infinitely many primes $p$.

*Conclusion.* Fix $a$, and take such a prime $p$ with $p>a$ and $a+p>C$. Then $a+kp=a+f(p)$ divides $a^2+pf(a)$, and it also divides $a(a+kp)=a^2+kpa$. Subtracting, $a+kp\mid p\,(f(a)-ka)$. Since $\gcd(a+kp,p)=\gcd(a,p)=1$, we get $a+kp\mid f(a)-ka$. This holds for infinitely many primes $p$, and $a+kp$ grows without bound, so $f(a)-ka=0$.

**Answer: $f(a)=ka$ for some positive integer $k$, whatever the value of $C$.**

prompt: Let $a$ be a positive integer. We say that a positive integer $b$ is *$a$-good* if $\binom{an}{b}-1$ is divisible by $an+1$ for all positive integers $n$ with $an\ge b$. Suppose $b$ is a positive integer such that $b$ is $a$-good, but $b+2$ is not $a$-good. Prove that $b+1$ is prime.
answer: Proof: $b$ is $a$-good iff $b$ is even and every prime $p\le b$ divides $a$. Then $b$ even with all $p\le b$ dividing $a$, while some prime $q\le b+2$ does not divide $a$; so $q=b+1$, since $b+2$ is even.

solutions.title: Characterise the $a$-good numbers
solutions.body:
The condition $an+1\mid\binom{an}b-1$ says
$$\frac{an(an-1)\cdots(an-b+1)}{b!}\equiv1\pmod{an+1}.\tag{1}$$

**Claim.** $b$ is $a$-good if and only if $b$ is even and $p\mid a$ for every prime $p\le b$.

*If some prime $p\le b$ does not divide $a$, then $b$ is not $a$-good.* Let $t=v_p(b!)$. Since $p\nmid a$, there is $c>0$ with $ac\equiv1\pmod{p^{t+1}}$; enlarge $c$ by multiples of $p^{t+1}$ so that $n=(p-1)c$ satisfies $an\ge b$. Then $an\equiv p-1\pmod{p^{t+1}}$. Since $p-1\le b-1$, the factor $an-(p-1)$ occurs in the numerator $an(an-1)\cdots(an-b+1)$, and it is divisible by $p^{t+1}$. So $v_p$ of the numerator is at least $t+1>t=v_p(b!)$, and $p\mid\binom{an}b$. But $an+1\equiv p\equiv0\pmod p$, so $p\mid an+1$, while $\binom{an}b-1\equiv-1\pmod p$. Hence $an+1\nmid\binom{an}b-1$.

*If every prime $p\le b$ divides $a$.* Then every prime factor of $b!$ divides $a$ and so does not divide $an+1$; thus $b!$ is invertible modulo $an+1$. Since $an-j\equiv-1-j\pmod{an+1}$, (1) becomes
$$(-1)^b\,b!\equiv b!\pmod{an+1}.$$
For even $b$ this holds for every $n$, so $b$ is $a$-good. For odd $b$ it says $an+1\mid2\cdot b!$, which fails once $an+1>2\cdot b!$; so $b$ is not $a$-good. This proves the claim.

**Conclusion.** Since $b$ is $a$-good, $b$ is even and every prime $\le b$ divides $a$. The number $b+2$ is also even and not $a$-good, so by the claim some prime $q\le b+2$ does not divide $a$. Necessarily $q>b$, so $q\in\{b+1,b+2\}$. But $b+2\ge4$ is even, hence not prime. So $q=b+1$, i.e. $b+1$ is prime. ∎

prompt: Let $H=\big\{\lfloor i\sqrt2\rfloor:\ i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\big\}=\{1,2,4,5,7,\dots\}$, and let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exists a constant $C$ such that, if $A\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ satisfies $|A|\ge C\sqrt n$, then there exist $a,b\in A$ such that $a-b\in H$. (Here $\mathbb Z_{>0}$ is the set of positive integers, and $\lfloor z\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $z$.)
answer: Proof: $m\in H\iff\{m/\sqrt2\}>1-\frac1{\sqrt2}$. If no difference lies in $H$, then after shifting $\min A$ to $0$ the fractional parts $\{a_i/\sqrt2\}$ increase with $a_i$ and stay below $1-\frac1{\sqrt2}$; since $\{d/\sqrt2\}>\frac1{2\sqrt2\,d}$, AM–HM gives $(|A|-1)^2<(2\sqrt2-2)n$. So $C=1+\sqrt{2\sqrt2-2}$ works.

solutions.title: Fractional parts of multiples of $1/\sqrt2$
solutions.body:
We show that if no difference of two elements of $A$ lies in $H$, then $|A|<1+\sqrt{(2\sqrt2-2)n}$. Hence $C=1+\sqrt{2\sqrt2-2}$ works, as $1\le\sqrt n$.

**Membership test.** For a positive integer $m$,
$$m\in H\iff\Big\{\frac m{\sqrt2}\Big\}>1-\frac1{\sqrt2}.\tag{1}$$
Indeed, $m\in H$ iff $m<i\sqrt2<m+1$ for some integer $i$ (equality is impossible since $\sqrt2$ is irrational), i.e. iff the open interval $\big(\frac m{\sqrt2},\frac m{\sqrt2}+\frac1{\sqrt2}\big)$ contains an integer. The first integer above $\frac m{\sqrt2}$ is $\frac m{\sqrt2}+1-\{\frac m{\sqrt2}\}$, which gives (1). Equality in (1) would make $\frac{m+1}{\sqrt2}$ an integer, which is impossible.

**A lower bound.** For a positive integer $d$, let $h=\lfloor d/\sqrt2\rfloor$. Then
$$\Big\{\frac d{\sqrt2}\Big\}\Big(\frac d{\sqrt2}+h\Big)=\frac{d^2}2-h^2=\frac{d^2-2h^2}2\ge\frac12,$$
since $d^2-2h^2$ is a positive integer. As $\frac d{\sqrt2}+h<\frac{2d}{\sqrt2}$,
$$\Big\{\frac d{\sqrt2}\Big\}>\frac1{2\sqrt2\,d}.\tag{2}$$

**Ordering the fractional parts.** Let $A=\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}$ have no difference in $H$. Differences don't change under translation, so assume $a_1=0$ and $a_k\le n-1$. By (1), $\{a_i/\sqrt2\}<1-\frac1{\sqrt2}$ for $i>1$, and this also holds for $i=1$.

For $i<j$ we must have $\{a_i/\sqrt2\}<\{a_j/\sqrt2\}$. These are never equal, by irrationality. If instead $\{a_i/\sqrt2\}>\{a_j/\sqrt2\}$, then
$$\Big\{\frac{a_j-a_i}{\sqrt2}\Big\}=\Big\{\frac{a_j}{\sqrt2}\Big\}-\Big\{\frac{a_i}{\sqrt2}\Big\}+1>1-\Big(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\Big)=\frac1{\sqrt2}>1-\frac1{\sqrt2},$$
so $a_j-a_i\in H$ by (1), which is excluded.

**Counting.** Let $d_i=a_{i+1}-a_i$ for $1\le i<k$. Since the fractional parts increase, $\{a_{i+1}/\sqrt2\}-\{a_i/\sqrt2\}\in(0,1)$ is congruent to $d_i/\sqrt2$ modulo $1$, so it equals $\{d_i/\sqrt2\}$. Telescoping and using (2) and the AM–HM inequality:
$$1-\frac1{\sqrt2}>\Big\{\frac{a_k}{\sqrt2}\Big\}=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\Big\{\frac{d_i}{\sqrt2}\Big\}>\frac1{2\sqrt2}\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac1{d_i}\ge\frac{(k-1)^2}{2\sqrt2\sum_id_i}>\frac{(k-1)^2}{2\sqrt2\,n},$$
because $\sum d_i=a_k<n$. (For $k=1$ the bound below is trivial.) Thus $(k-1)^2<(2\sqrt2-2)\,n$, i.e.
$$|A|=k<1+\sqrt{2\sqrt2-2}\,\sqrt n\le\big(1+\sqrt{2\sqrt2-2}\big)\sqrt n .$$
So any $A$ with $|A|\ge C\sqrt n$, $C=1+\sqrt{2\sqrt2-2}$, contains $a,b$ with $a-b\in H$. ∎

prompt: Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ and infinitely many positive integers $n$ with the following property: there are infinitely many positive integers that cannot be expressed as the sum of fewer than $cn\log(n)$ pairwise coprime $n^{\text{th}}$ powers.
answer: Proof: take primes $p\mid2^{2^{t-1}}+1$, $q\mid2^{2^t}+1$ and $n=\frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{2^t}$, $N=pq$. Then $n$-th powers are $0$ or $1$ mod $p$ and mod $q$, so sums of $j$ pairwise coprime $n$-th powers take at most $4$ residues mod $N$. Since $N>\frac12n\log_2n$, a residue class is missed when $j<\frac18n\ln n$.

solutions.title: Few residues modulo a product of Fermat-number primes
solutions.body:
We use the natural logarithm and show that $c=\frac18$ works.

**Construction.** Fix $t\ge1$ and choose primes $p\mid2^{2^{t-1}}+1$ and $q\mid2^{2^t}+1$. They are distinct, since distinct Fermat numbers are coprime. From $2^{2^{t-1}}\equiv-1\pmod p$, the order of $2$ modulo $p$ is exactly $2^t$, so $2^t\mid p-1$; similarly $2^{t+1}\mid q-1$. Put
$$N=pq,\qquad n=\frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{2^t}.$$
Here $n$ is an integer, $p-1\mid n$ (as $\frac{q-1}{2^t}$ is an integer), and $q-1\mid n$ (as $\frac{p-1}{2^t}$ is an integer). Also $n\ge\frac{2^t\cdot2^{t+1}}{2^t}=2^{t+1}$, so letting $t$ grow gives infinitely many $n$.

**Residues.** By Fermat's little theorem, an $n$-th power is $\equiv1\pmod p$ if it is coprime to $p$, and $\equiv0$ otherwise. In a sum of $j$ pairwise coprime $n$-th powers at most one term is divisible by $p$, so the sum is $\equiv j$ or $j-1\pmod p$; the same holds mod $q$. By the Chinese remainder theorem, such sums lie in at most $4$ residue classes mod $N$ for each $j$. So sums of at most $m$ pairwise coprime $n$-th powers occupy at most $4m$ residue classes mod $N$. If $4m<N$, some class mod $N$ contains no such sum, and its infinitely many positive members are not expressible.

**Size.** We have $p\le2^{2^{t-1}}+1$ and $q\le2^{2^t}+1$, so $\log_2n\le2^{t-1}+2^t-t<2^{t+1}$. Also $\frac Nn=\frac{pq\,2^t}{(p-1)(q-1)}>2^t$. Hence $\log_2n<\frac{2N}n$, i.e.
$$N>\tfrac12\,n\log_2n=\frac{n\ln n}{2\ln2}>\tfrac12\,n\ln n .$$

**Conclusion.** Let $m$ be the largest integer below $\frac18n\ln n$; sums of fewer than $\frac18n\ln n$ terms have at most $m$ terms. Then $4m<\frac12n\ln n<N$. So for each of the infinitely many $n$ above, infinitely many positive integers are not sums of fewer than $\frac18n\ln n$ pairwise coprime $n$-th powers. ∎

prompt:
Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive integers. Prove that the integer
$$a^2+\left\lceil\frac{4a^2}b\right\rceil$$
is not a square. (Here $\lceil z\rceil$ denotes the least integer greater than or equal to $z$.)
answer: Proof by descent: a square $(a+k)^2$ gives a positive solution of $\lceil c^2/b\rceil=(c+k)k$ (with $c=2a$). For the one with least $k$, $bk<c<bk+k$, so $c=bk+r$ with $0<r<k$, and $(c',k')=(r,k-r)$ is a solution with smaller $k$.

solutions.title: Infinite descent
solutions.body:
Suppose $a^2+\lceil4a^2/b\rceil=(a+k)^2$. Since $\lceil4a^2/b\rceil\ge1$, $k\ge1$, and $\lceil(2a)^2/b\rceil=2ak+k^2=(2a+k)k$. So the equation
$$\Big\lceil\frac{c^2}b\Big\rceil=(c+k)k\tag{1}$$
has a solution in positive integers $(c,k)$. Among all positive solutions, take one with $k$ minimal (no parity condition on $c$ is needed).

**Locating $c$.** From (1),
$$\frac{c^2}b>\Big\lceil\frac{c^2}b\Big\rceil-1=ck+k^2-1\ge ck,$$
so $c>bk$. Also
$$\frac{(c-k)(c+k)}b<\frac{c^2}b\le(c+k)k,$$
so $c-k<bk$. Hence $bk<c<bk+k$, which forces $k\ge2$, and $c=bk+r$ with $0<r<k$.

**Descent.** Substituting,
$$\Big\lceil\frac{c^2}b\Big\rceil=\Big\lceil\frac{(bk+r)^2}b\Big\rceil=bk^2+2kr+\Big\lceil\frac{r^2}b\Big\rceil,\qquad(c+k)k=bk^2+rk+k^2 .$$
So by (1)
$$\Big\lceil\frac{r^2}b\Big\rceil=k^2-kr=k(k-r)=\big(r+(k-r)\big)(k-r).$$
Thus $(c',k')=(r,k-r)$ is another positive solution of (1) with $0<k'<k$, contradicting the minimality of $k$. Hence $a^2+\lceil4a^2/b\rceil$ is never a square. ∎
